papers.title: Substrate insulated Josephson junctions for superconducting quantum circuits
papers.abstract: We have developed a fabrication technique for Josephson junctions that employs a three-dimensional patterned, low-loss substrate instead of commonly used organic resists. The technique enables the fabrication of high-quality trilayer junctions from a wide range of geometries and materials, including high-melting-point superconductors such as tantalum or niobium. The junction electrodes are free from intentionally introduced oxides and organic materials, which are known sources of decoherence. We fabricate and characterize underdamped Nb/AlOx/Nb junctions of different sizes in several geometries. Such junctions enable manufacturing of quantum circuits operating at higher speeds and elevated temperatures.

summary.summary: This work develops a substrate-patterned fabrication technique for Josephson junctions that eliminates organic resists and intentional oxides near the junction by using three-dimensional step-and-undercut geometries etched into the substrate. The approach enables high-quality underdamped Nb/AlOx/Nb junctions across multiple geometries (step-edge insulated, cross-step insulated, Manhattan trench, and cross-trench) without lossy dielectric contamination, achieving $J_c R_n$ values of ~1.6 mV and $R_{sg}/R_n$ up to ~50.
summary.motivation: High-melting-point superconductors like Nb and Ta can enable JJs operating above 300 mK and beyond 40 GHz, but conventional fabrication using organic resist lift-off fails at their higher deposition temperatures, while magnetron sputtering junctions suffer from nearby lossy dielectric layers that introduce excess noise.
summary.method: Josephson junctions are fabricated by depositing trilayers (M1/TB1/M2) onto patterned Si substrates featuring step-and-undercut geometries that electrically isolate the junction electrodes; multiple implementations (SEI, cSEI, p-cSEI, MT, cT) are demonstrated with varying trench depths ($\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ in the range 100–450 nm) and material combinations, characterized via DC I-V measurements and microwave resonator quality factors.
summary.result: SEI junctions with area $A = 100$ µm² exhibit $I_c = 110$ µA, $R_n = 12.7$ Ω, $V_g = 2.78$ mV, and pronounced hysteresis with low retrapping current; Nb CPW resonators show internal quality factors exceeding $3 \times 10^5$ at ~7 GHz; critical current density varies with oxidation parameters following a power law, with $J_c$ values ranging from 0.4 to 24.7 µA/µm² and effective undercut parameter $u$ from 0 to 1.4 µm across fabrication runs.

papers.title: Logical error estimation from syndrome data of surface-code experiments
papers.abstract: Decoders for quantum error correction (QEC) experiments rely on detector error models (DEMs), which encode, for each error, its probability and the detectors and logical observables it flips. Here we show that estimating DEM event probabilities from experimental syndromes is feasible, avoids independent device benchmarking, and produces useful decoder priors for estimating and reducing decoded logical error probabilities. We evaluate our methods using open-source data from surface-code memory experiments performed on Google's Willow chip, and we carry out analogous surface-code experiments on IBM's \texttt{ibm\_miami} processor. Despite the different physical error scales of the Google and IBM devices, in both cases our estimated DEMs improve logical error probabilities relative to baseline device-informed DEMs, typically at the $5\%-10\%$ level and with larger gains in some IBM cases, without additional calibration circuits, decoder fine-tuning, or supervised fitting to logical outcomes.

summary.summary: This work demonstrates that detector error model (DEM) event probabilities for surface-code decoders can be estimated directly from experimental syndrome data without separate calibration or device benchmarking. Syndrome-estimated DEMs reduce logical error probabilities by 5%–10% relative to baseline device-informed DEMs on both Google's Willow chip (rotated ZXXZ surface code with $d\in\{3,5,7\}$) and IBM's ibm_miami processor (unrotated code with $d=3$), reaching ~38% improvement in single-cycle cases on IBM without requiring additional circuits or supervised fitting.
summary.motivation: Standard DEM characterization methods such as tomography do not scale to large QEC systems, and prior Pauli noise-learning approaches require extra pre-optimization circuits. Recent theoretical work suggested syndrome-based DEM estimation is feasible, but decoder-level logical performance across multiple devices, distances, and cycle counts remained unexplored.
summary.method: DEM event probabilities on fixed reference detector-logical supports are estimated from empirical detector moments and covariances computed over 50,000 experimental shots per case, using hierarchical inversion formulas for graphlike and hyperedge rates (equations 17–26). Logical error probabilities are then evaluated by decoding experimental syndromes with MWPM using these estimated DEMs, compared against SI1000 circuit-level and RL-optimized baseline DEMs.
summary.result: For Willow across nine subsystems and $d\in\{3,5,7\}$ with $r\in\{1,10,13,30,50,70\}$ cycles, syndrome-estimated DEMs yield $\Delta P_L$ values typically $\lesssim -10\%$ relative to SI1000 and perform comparably to RL-optimized DEMs; for ibm_miami at $d=3$ with $r\leq19$ cycles, syndrome-estimated DEMs reduce logical error probabilities 5%–10% relative to IBM-like baseline, with larger gains when dynamical decoupling eliminates coherent errors and negative detector covariances.
